title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance + ADRs
author: Aisha Kapoor
body:
Purpose
-------
This document consolidates Redwood Inference's canonical architecture and engineering standards for API design, coding practices, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, and performance. It also includes a small set of Decision Records (ADRs) that capture recently approved architecture trade-offs. The intent is to provide a single reference engineers can use when designing services, model endpoints, and operational runbooks.

Scope
-----
Applies to all Redwood-owned services and customer-facing components across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments, including: API endpoints, model-serving runtime components, infra provisioning artifacts, and observability/alerting configurations. Does not replace team-level implementation details but provides mandatory organizational defaults.

Ownership
---------
- Standards steward: eng-architecture (primary)
- Implementation owners: service-level engineering teams
- Review cadence: quarterly (standards), ADRs reviewed at triage every release

1) API Standards
----------------
Intro: APIs are the primary integration surface for customers and internal services. Our standards optimize for stability, discoverability, and predictable error semantics.

API design principles:
- Use RESTful resources for CRUD-like operations; use gRPC for high-throughput internal RPCs where binary payloads or streaming are required.
- Version every public API (major.minor). Major version changes require migration guides and a deprecation period of at least 90 days.
- Use consistent HTTP status conventions: 2xx success, 4xx client errors, 5xx server errors. Map common platform errors to documented codes.
- All request/response schemas must be specified in OpenAPI 3.1 and validated in CI.
- Support both request-level and streaming response patterns for generation/chat endpoints. For streaming, use chunked transfer with an explicit finalization message.

Security & data handling:
- TLS 1.2+ mandatory for all endpoints.
- PII-containing fields must be labelled in schemas and encrypted at rest using customer or Redwood KMS as appropriate. See security-and-compliance/access-and-permissions for integration details.

API contract checklist (to include in PR):
1. OpenAPI spec included and generator-compatible.
2. Schema examples for success/error responses.
3. Rate limit behavior documented.
4. Backwards-compatibility notes (breaking/non-breaking changes).

Example OpenAPI snippet (bookkeeping only):
```
paths:
  /v1/generate:
    post:
      summary: Generate text
      requestBody: { ... }
      responses:
        '200': { description: OK, content: { 'application/json': { schema: { $ref: '#/components/schemas/GenerationResponse' } } } }
```

2) Coding Standards
--------------------
Goals: Readable, testable, consistent code across services with clear ownership and automated checks.

Language and style defaults:
- Primary languages: Go (services), Python (model tooling, evals), TypeScript (console/frontend).
- Formatting and linting: enforce gofmt/golangci-lint for Go, black/ruff for Python, eslint + prettier for TypeScript. CI must fail on lint/format errors.
- Import ordering and module boundaries: prefer small, focused packages; avoid cyclical imports.

Testing:
- Unit tests: target >= 70% coverage for new service packages; critical infra and runtime components target >= 85%.
- Integration tests: include at least one end-to-end integration test per public API surface that runs in CI against a staging instance.
- Contract tests: API consumers and providers use contract tests generated from OpenAPI schemas.

Code review & PR requirements:
- PR description must include design rationale, changelog entry, and which teams are impacted.
- Two approvals required from different teams for cross-team API changes.
- ADR required for any design that changes runtime behavior or the model-serving pipeline.

3) Infrastructure Standards
--------------------------
Provisioning:
- Use Terraform as the canonical IaC tool. Modules must follow the shared-modules pattern in eng-infra/terraform-and-iac.
- All production-level changes must go through a pipeline with a plan review step. No direct console edits in production.

Networking & security:
- VPC-per-environment with private subnets for compute that handle customer data. Public-facing proxies in segmented DMZs.
- Use mTLS for internal service-to-service communication where feasible.
- Secrets must be stored in KMS-backed secret managers (AWS Secrets Manager / GCP Secret Manager) with rotation policies.

Capacity & scaling:
- Autoscaling rules must include graceful scale-in cooldowns and minimum instance counts to maintain warm caches for model-serving (defaults: min 2 pods per zone for critical services).
- GPU fleet tagging: every GPU node must include tags for generation (gpu:yes), hardware (A100-v5), region, and owner_team.

Disaster recovery:
- Daily automated backups for critical stateful components (metadata DBs, model registry). Recovery RTO/RPO defined in service-level SLO docs.

4) Model-serving Standards
--------------------------
Objectives: safely serve models with predictable latency and throughput while enabling model rollouts and versioning.

Endpoint semantics:
- Each model rollout exposes immutable model-version endpoints (e.g., /models/llama-3-v1/...).
- Backwards-compatible model transforms (tokenizer changes, prompt formatting) must be accompanied by a conversion layer rather than changing existing endpoints.

Serving runtime configuration:
- Default container image base: redwood/runtime-base:stable-2026-01.
- Preferred hardware profiles documented in eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity (e.g., 8xA100 for batching-heavy workloads, 4xH100 for low-latency single-token throughput).
- Quantization profiles: include pre-approved quant configs per model family in quantization-profiles; teams must not deploy ad-hoc quantized builds without quantization review.

Rollouts & experiments:
- Canary rollout: 5% traffic for 24 hours then 25% for 24 hours before full traffic. Fail-fast monitors will rollback automatically on defined quality/regression signals.
- A/B tests: traffic split must be captured in the experiment registry and tied to evaluation prompt sets.

Operational controls:
- Prefix and KV cache controls exposed as runtime knobs with documented defaults.
- Circuit breakers: per-endpoint token cost and 99th percentile latency thresholds that trigger progressive throttling and fallback to smaller model variants.

5) Observability Standards
-------------------------
Goal: make it easy to detect, triage, and attribute regressions in latency, cost, and quality.

Metrics (all services):
- Request-level: request_count, request_latency_ms (p50/p90/p99), request_size_tokens, response_size_tokens, response_error_count.
- Model-level: tokens_generated_total, kv_cache_hit_ratio, batch_size_distribution, model_load_time_ms.
- Cost metrics: estimated_cost_per_1k_tokens, gpu_seconds_used.

Tracing & logs:
- Use OpenTelemetry for traces and propagate trace context across service boundaries.
- Structured JSON logs with keys: timestamp, service, trace_id, span_id, request_id, user_tier, model_version, latency_ms, error (if any).
- Log retention: default 30 days for app logs, 365 days for audit logs (configurable by plan).

Dashboards & alerts:
- Default dashboard per service: overview (SLOs), latency heatmap, error breakdown, cost by route.
- Alerting thresholds (default):
  - Page on P99 latency > 6000ms for generation endpoints for 3m sustained.
  - Page on error rate > 2% for 5m sustained or any spike with critical customer impact.
  - Ticket for cost anomalies: > 30% daily increase vs 7d rolling baseline.

Alerting runbook linkage: every alert must link to a runbook in eng-platform/runbooks with severity and escalation steps.

6) Performance Standards
------------------------
SLOs & targets (company defaults):
- Latency SLOs (per plan):
  - Free/Dev: p95 <= 1.5s, p99 <= 6s.
  - Production/Business: p95 <= 500ms, p99 <= 2000ms.
- Throughput: publish per-model throughput profile on the model catalog page.
- Cost targets: teams must track estimated cost per 1k tokens and provide optimizations for any endpoint with cost > $0.10 per 1k tokens (hosted pricing benchmark).

Benchmarking and perf testing:
- Every new model and major config change must run the perf-suite (eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite) and produce a perf report that includes latency distribution across sequence lengths, memory footprint, and effective throughput with baseline hardware.
- Benchmarks must be reproducible and checked into the model-onboarding folder with a perf-report.md.

7) Decision Records (ADRs)
--------------------------
This section records recent architectural choices and their rationale. ADRs are immutable once published; updates must be added as new ADRs referencing the prior.

ADR-2026-01: Default to OpenAPI for public API contracts
- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-02-20
- Context: Need a human- and tool-readable contract that integrates with SDK generation and contract tests.
- Decision: Use OpenAPI 3.1 as canonical format for all public REST surfaces; gRPC allowed for internal high-throughput services.
- Consequences: CI enforces OpenAPI presence; SDK generation pipeline added to eng-developer-experience.

ADR-2026-02: Model-versioned endpoints and immutable model objects
- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-03-15
- Context: Frequent tokenizer and micro-formatting changes caused silent behavior regressions for customers.
- Decision: Expose immutable model-version endpoints and require conversion layers when changing input/output contracts.
- Consequences: Slightly higher surface area for model endpoints but stronger isolation for rollouts and easier regression triage.

ADR-2026-03: Quantization profiles controlled by applied-ml team
- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-04-01
- Context: Quantization can affect output quality in subtle ways; ad-hoc quantization led to reproducibility issues.
- Decision: Centralize approved quantization profiles; deployments must reference a profile id.
- Consequences: Slower iteration for teams exploring quantization but improved traceability and rollbacks.

8) Operationalizing the standards
--------------------------------
Checklist for adopting these standards when authoring a new service or model endpoint:
1. Add OpenAPI spec and contract tests to the repo.
2. Include perf-suite bench and perf-report in model onboarding.
3. Add instrumentation for required metrics and tracing.
4. Create a Terraform module or use existing shared module for infra.
5. Register model/version in model registry and experiment registry if running A/B tests.
6. Link deployment to rollback-enabled CI/CD pipeline and automated canary policy.

Appendix: Templates and examples
-------------------------------
- PR template: include API changes, migration notes, perf summary, and estimated cost delta.
- Runbook snippet: include quick triage checklist, how to rollback model versions, and whom to page.
- OpenAPI checklist table:
  | Item | Required | Owner |
  |------|----------|-------|
  | OpenAPI spec present | Yes | API owner |
  | Examples for success + errors | Yes | API owner |
  | Rate-limit and quota notes | Yes | Product/Platform |
